gloss: live; living, alive; life; living thing, beast
summary: The root is to live, to be alive and not dead: scripture sets it against מוּת “die” from Gen 2 to Dan 12. The verb is to live, to stay alive, to recover from sickness, and to live again from death; in the piel and hiphil to keep alive and to make alive, which is Yahweh's own work (“I put to death and I make alive”, Deu 32:39). חַי is living or alive, of man, beast, running water and raw flesh, and above all of God, “the living God”, by whose life men swear; חַיִּים is life, breathed into man's nostrils by God, set before Israel with death to choose between, and promised as “life of the age” to those who wake from the dust (Dan 12:2); חַיָּה is a living thing, usually the wild beast. Man and beast alike are נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, “living soul” (Gen 1:20–24; 2:7). Daniel's Aramaic and the Peshitta have the same root, the Peshitta using it also for “save” and “Saviour”; Arabic, Ugaritic, Phoenician and Sabaic share it.

words.gloss: living, alive; the living; (of water) running; (of flesh) raw
words.summary: The adjective, feminine חַיָּה, plural חַיִּים, and as a noun “the living”. Its construct חֵי (חַי before the divine name) makes the oath “by the life of”. It shares its spelling with forms of the verb (חַי “he lived”, Gen 5:5) and its plural with the noun חַיִּים “life”, so the count of its uses cannot be separated exactly from theirs.

senses.definition: Of a man or an animal: having life, not dead. It is asked and told of the absent (“is your father still alive?”), said of those taken or swallowed alive, and set against the dead one.

evidence.note: The two mothers: “my son is הַחַי and your son is הַמֵּת”: living is the opposite of dead.
“Is your father still חַי?”
“Joseph is still חַי.”
Moses would see whether his brothers in Egypt are still חַיִּים.
“While the child was still חַי I fasted and wept.”
Elijah gives the child back to his mother: “See, your son is חַי.”
The king of Ai they took חָי, alive.
The goat for Azazel is stood חַי before Yahweh.
Korah's company “go down חַיִּים to Sheol”: alive into the grave, the ground closing over them (16:33).
“Then they would have swallowed us חַיִּים.”
“A חַי dog is better than the dead lion.”
אָדָם חָי, “a living man”.
“I know that my redeemer is חָי.”

senses.definition: As a noun: those who are alive, set against the dead; כָּל־חַי, all that lives, man and beast together or mankind.

evidence.note: Aaron “stood between הַמֵּתִים and הַחַיִּים, and the plague was stayed”.
“הַחַיִּים know that they will die, but the dead know nothing.”
Hezekiah, recovered: “חַי חַי, he gives you thanks, as I do this day”; the grave cannot (38:18).
Eve is “the mother of כָּל־חָי”, all living: here, all mankind.
“I will not again strike כָּל־חַי”: every living thing, the beasts with man.
“Of all הָחַי, of all flesh, two of each.”
“You satisfy the desire of כָל־חַי.”
“In whose hand is the soul of כָּל־חָי and the breath of all flesh of man.”
“On behalf of הַחַיִּים, to the dead?”
אֶרֶץ חַיִּים, “land of the living”: the world of those alive.
The servant “was cut off from the land of the living”: he died.
“He is not God of the dead but of the living (Peshitta דּחַיֵא)”, said to prove that the dead are raised (20:37).

senses.definition: With נֶפֶשׁ: נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, “living soul”, the creature that breathes and moves. It is said first of the swarms of the water, then of the beasts of the earth, then of the man, and of all of them together in the covenant after the flood.

evidence.note: “Let the waters swarm with swarms of נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה.”
“Let the earth bring forth נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה after its kind: cattle, creeping thing and beast of earth.”
“The man became נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה”: the same two words as for the animals.
Whatever the man called each נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, that was its name.
The covenant is with “every נֶפֶשׁ הַחַיָּה that is with you, bird, cattle and every beast of the earth”.
Every נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה that swarms lives where the river comes.
Gen 2:7 quoted: the first man Adam became “a living soul” (ψυχὴν ζῶσαν; Peshitta לַנפֵֿש חַיָא).
“Every living soul died in the sea.”

senses.definition: Of God: אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, אֱלֹהִים חַי, אֵל חַי, “living God”. He speaks out of the fire, drives out nations, saves and judges, where the gods of the nations have no breath in them.

evidence.note: “Yahweh is God in truth; he is אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים and king of the age”, against the idols that cannot speak or walk and have no breath in them (10:5, 14).
“Who of all flesh has heard the voice of אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived (וַיֶּחִי)?”
“By this you shall know that אֵל חַי is among you”: he will drive out the nations.
The Philistine has reproached “the ranks of אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים”.
Sennacherib sent to reproach אֱלֹהִים חַי.
“It shall be said to them, sons of אֵל־חָי.”
“My soul thirsts for God, for אֵל חָי.”
“חַי־יַהְוֶה, and blessed be my rock.”
“You are the Christ, the son of the living God (Peshitta דַּאלָהָא חַיָא).”
Hos 2:1 quoted: “sons of the living God”.

senses.definition: In an oath: חַי־יַהְוֶה, “Yahweh is living”, by which a man swears; חֵי נַפְשְׁךָ, חֵי פַרְעֹה, “by the life of” a man; and Yahweh's own oath, חַי־אָנִי, “I am living”. The oath stakes what is sworn on a life that is sure.

evidence.note: “You shall swear, חַי־יַהְוֶה, in truth, in judgment and in righteousness.”
Saul: “for חַי־יַהְוֶה who saves Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.”
“חַי־יַהְוֶה וְחֵי נַפְשֶׁךָ, there is but a step between me and death”: Yahweh is “living”, the man has “life”.
Ittai: “חַי־יַהְוֶה וְחֵי אֲדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ … whether for death or for life, there your servant will be.”
Joseph swears as an Egyptian: חֵי פַרְעֹה.
The false oath: “חֵי your god, Dan.”
Yahweh's oath: “חַי־אָנִי, and all the earth shall be filled with the glory of Yahweh.”
“I lift my hand to heaven and say, חַי אָנֹכִי לְעֹלָם”: he swears by his own life, which is for ever.
“חַי־אָנִי, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live.”
The man in linen “swore by חֵי הָעוֹלָם”, him who lives for ever.
“As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me”: the oath formula joined to Isa 45:23.

senses.definition: Of water: מַיִם חַיִּים, “living water”, the water of a spring or stream that flows, against the still water of a cistern. The law requires it for cleansing; the prophets make it a figure of Yahweh.

evidence.note: Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found “a well of מַיִם חַיִּים”: a spring.
“They have forsaken me, the fountain of מַיִם חַיִּים, to hew themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that hold no water.”
The bird for the cleansed leper is killed over מַיִם חַיִּים.
מַיִם חַיִּים is put on the ashes of the sin offering.
“In that day מַיִם־חַיִּים shall go out from Jerusalem”, summer and winter.
Jesus at the well offers “living water” (Peshitta מַיָא חַיֵא).

senses.gloss: raw; (of flesh in a sore) quick
senses.definition: Of flesh: uncooked meat; and in the law of leprosy בָּשָׂר חַי, the “living” flesh that shows raw in a swelling.

evidence.note: The priest's servant: “he will not take boiled meat from you, but חָי”: raw is the opposite of cooked.
“On the day בָּשָׂר חַי appears in him he shall be unclean.”

senses.gloss: (at the time) living: a year on
senses.definition: In כָּעֵת חַיָּה, “at the time (when it is) living”: when this season comes round alive again, a year from now. Only of the promise of a son to Sarah and to the Shunammite.

evidence.note: “I will surely return to you כָּעֵת חַיָּה, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.”
“At the set time (לַמּוֹעֵד) I will return to you, כָּעֵת חַיָּה.”
“At this set time, כָּעֵת חַיָּה, you shall embrace a son”; she bore him “at that set time, כָּעֵת חַיָּה” (4:17).

evidence.locator: חַי → ζάω ×185 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Gen.2.7 לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה → εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν

evidence.note: Gen 2:7 quoted: εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν, “a living soul”.
Hos 2:1 quoted: υἱοὶ θεοῦ ζῶντος.
The son of the living God.
ζῶ ἐγώ, “as I live”: the oath חַי־אָנִי.
ὕδωρ ζῶν, living water.

opposites.note: The dead one, or the dead, set against the living.

phrases.gloss: living soul: a living creature, animal or man
living God (also אֱלֹהִים חַי, אֵל חַי)
“Yahweh is living”: the oath by Yahweh
“I am living”: Yahweh's oath by himself
the land of the living

evidence.note: Hezekiah, at the gates of Sheol: “I shall not see Yah in the land of the living.”

phrases.gloss: living water: running water
all living, every living thing
at this time next year

words.gloss: live; stay alive; recover; live again; (piel, hiphil) keep alive, make alive
words.summary: About 280 times: some 200 in the qal, 55 in the piel and 23 in the hiphil. The qal perfect is often חַי (וָחַי, Gen 3:22; Lev 18:5), spelt as the adjective, and the brief's count for the verb takes in many tokens of the adjective for that reason. Piel and hiphil overlap: both are to keep alive and to make alive.

stems.gloss: live, be alive; stay alive, survive; live by; recover, revive; live again

senses.gloss: live, be alive; live so many years
senses.definition: To be alive, to have life and pass one's days: the genealogies count how long each man lived before and after he fathered his son, and then that he died.

evidence.note: “Adam וַיְחִי a hundred and thirty years and fathered a son.”
“All the days of Adam which he חַי were nine hundred and thirty years, and he died.”
Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years.
“What man יִחְיֶה and shall not see death, shall deliver his soul from the hand of Sheol?”: no man lives on without dying.
“Lest he take also of the tree of life and eat וָחַי לְעֹלָם, and live for ever.”
“O that Ishmael might live before you!”

senses.definition: To go on living where death threatens: through famine, war, sickness or the judgment of God; often “live and not die”, and of the soul, “my soul shall live”.

evidence.note: “Buy for us from there, וְנִחְיֶה וְלֹא נָמוּת, that we may live and not die.”
“That my soul may live because of you.”
“He will pray for you, and live; and if you do not restore her, know that you shall surely die.”
“Man shall not see me וָחָי, and live.”
Everyone bitten, when he sees the serpent on the pole, וָחָי: he does not die of the bite.
“Do this for them, that they may live and not die.”
“Let Reuben live and not die.”
He who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live, “and his soul shall be his for spoil”.
“I shall not die, but live, and tell the works of Yah.”

senses.definition: To have life as the outcome of hearing and doing what Yahweh says: the man who does his statutes shall live by them, the wicked who turns shall live and not die, and the righteous shall live by his faithfulness. Its opposite in every place is to die for one's sin.

evidence.note: “You shall keep my statutes and my judgments, which the man shall do וָחַי בָּהֶם, and live by them.”
“Not by bread alone does the man live, but by everything that goes out of the mouth of Yahweh does the man live.”
“The righteous בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ יִחְיֶה, by his faithfulness shall live”, against the man whose soul is puffed up.
The man who walks in Yahweh's statutes: “he is righteous, חָיֹה יִחְיֶה, he shall surely live.”
The wicked who turns from all his sins “shall surely live, he shall not die”.
“I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies: turn, and live.”
“Hear the statutes … that you may live, and go in and possess the land.”
“Choose life, that you may live, you and your seed.”
“Seek me, and live.”
“Hear, and your soul shall live.”
“Keep my commandments, and live.”
Hab 2:4 quoted: the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith.
Paul sets Hab 2:4 beside Lev 18:5: no one is justified by law, for “the righteous shall live by faith”, while the law says “he who does them shall live by them”.
Deu 8:3 quoted by Jesus in the wilderness.

senses.definition: To come back to health or strength: of the sick who recover, of wounds that heal, and of the spirit or heart that revives.

evidence.note: Ahaziah, fallen through the lattice: “whether אֶחְיֶה from this sickness”.
Hezekiah “was sick, וַיְחִי from his sickness”.
They laid the figs on the boil, וַיֶּחִי.
The circumcised stayed in the camp עַד חֲיוֹתָם, until they were healed.
“The spirit of Jacob their father וַתְּחִי, revived.”
Samson drank, “and his spirit returned, וַיֶּחִי”.
“May your heart live for ever.”

senses.definition: Of the dead: to come back to life. Scripture tells of dead who lived when a prophet prayed or when a body touched Elisha's bones, and promises it of Yahweh's dead, who shall rise from the dust.

evidence.note: “The soul of the child returned upon his inward part, וַיֶּחִי.”
The dead man touched the bones of Elisha, “וַיְחִי and stood up on his feet”.
“Your dead יִחְיוּ; my corpses shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in dust.”
Of the lords who ruled Israel: “dead, they shall not live; shades, they shall not rise.”
“If a man dies, הֲיִחְיֶה, shall he live? All the days of my service I will wait, until my change comes.”
“Son of man, shall these bones live?”
“The breath came into them, וַיִּחְיוּ, and they stood on their feet.”
“On the third day he will raise us up, וְנִחְיֶה before him.”
“He who believes in me, though he die, shall live” (Peshitta נִחֵא).
“They lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.”

senses.definition: The acclamation of a king, יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ, and the courtier's greeting, “may the king live for ever”.

evidence.note: At Saul's choosing all the people shouted, יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
At Joash's anointing they clapped and said, יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
Bathsheba: “May my lord king David live for ever.”

stems.gloss: keep alive, let live; make alive; revive; restore

senses.definition: To let someone live whom one might kill, or to keep a creature alive by feeding it: the opposite of killing.

evidence.note: “They will kill me, and you יְחַיּוּ, they will let live.”
The midwives “וַתְּחַיֶּיןָ the boys”, whom Pharaoh had said to kill.
“A sorceress you shall not let live.”
“You shall not let live anything that breathes.”
Joshua made a covenant with the Gibeonites לְחַיּוֹתָם.
The pairs are taken into the ark “to keep seed alive on the face of all the earth”.
“Perhaps we may find grass and keep horse and mule alive.”
The poor man's lamb, which he bought וַיְחַיֶּהָ: reared, kept alive.
“To deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine.”
The false prophetesses “put to death souls that should not die and keep alive souls that should not live”.
The wicked who turns “shall keep his soul alive”.

senses.definition: To give life: said of Yahweh, who gives life to all that he has made and who alone puts to death and makes alive.

evidence.note: “There is no god with me: I put to death וַאֲחַיֶּה; I have wounded, and I heal.”
“Yahweh puts to death וּמְחַיֶּה; he brings down to Sheol, and brings up”: to make alive is to bring up from the grave.
“You made the heavens, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them, וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת־כֻּלָּם.”
“The spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty תְּחַיֵּנִי.”
“After two days he will make us alive.”
“You brought up my soul from Sheol; חִיִּיתַנִי from among those going down to the pit.”
“You will make me alive again, and from the depths of the earth bring me up again.”
“Wisdom gives life to those who have it.”

senses.definition: To give new life to the afflicted: the prayer of Psalm 119, “revive me according to your word”, and of the people for themselves.

evidence.note: “My soul clings to the dust; חַיֵּנִי according to your word.”
“Your saying חִיָּתְנִי.”
“By your precepts you have given me life.”
“Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?”
“Yahweh, your work, in the midst of the years חַיֵּיהוּ.”

senses.definition: Of stones and a city: to bring them back from ruin, as if to life.

evidence.note: Sanballat: “will they הַיְחַיּוּ the stones out of the heaps of dust, burned as they are?”
David built the city round about, “and Joab יְחַיֶּה the rest of the city”.

stems.gloss: keep alive, let live; make alive

senses.gloss: keep alive, let live, save alive
senses.definition: As the piel: to preserve life that would otherwise be lost, in the ark, in famine, or in war.

evidence.note: Two of all flesh brought into the ark לְהַחֲיֹת, to keep alive.
“God sent me before you … לְהַחֲיוֹת for you a great escape.”
“God meant it for good, to keep alive a great people.”
The Egyptians to Joseph: “הֶחֱיִתָנוּ, you have kept us alive.”
“I would have killed you, and her I would have let live.”
Rahab and her father's house Joshua הֶחֱיָה.
Caleb: “Yahweh has kept me alive these forty-five years.”
David measured Moab: “two lines to put to death, and one full line לְהַחֲיוֹת.”

senses.definition: To give life to the dead or the dying, which belongs to God; and to revive the spirit of the lowly.

evidence.note: The king of Israel: “Am I God, to put to death וּלְהַחֲיוֹת, that this man sends to me to recover a man of his leprosy?”
Gehazi tells the king how Elisha הֶחֱיָה אֶת־הַמֵּת, “made the dead live”.
Hezekiah: “you restore me to health וְהַחֲיֵנִי.”
The high and holy one dwells with the crushed, “to revive the spirit of the lowly and to revive the heart of the crushed”.
Hab 2:4 quoted: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται.
Deu 8:3 quoted: οὐκ ἐπ᾽ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ἄνθρωπος.
Lev 18:5 quoted.
Lev 18:5 quoted.
“Do this, and you shall live.”

evidence.locator: 2Ki.5.7 לְהַחֲיוֹת → ζωοποιῆσαι; Neh.9.6 מְחַיֶּה → ζωοποιεῖς; Psa.71.20 תְּחַיֵּינִי → ἐζωοποίησάς; Job.36.6; Ecc.7.12; Jdg.21.14

evidence.note: “As the Father raises the dead and makes them alive, so the son makes alive whom he will.”
God, “who makes the dead alive”.
“In Christ shall all be made alive.”
The last Adam became “a life-giving spirit”.
“If a law had been given that could make alive.”

evidence.locator: Exo.1.18 תְּחַיֶּיןָ → ἐζωογονεῖτε; Exo.1.22; Jdg.8.19 הַחֲיִתֶם → ἐζωογονήκειτε; 1Sa.2.6 מְחַיֶּה → ζωογονεῖ; 1Ki.20.31; 2Ki.7.4

evidence.note: Stephen on Exo 1: Pharaoh made them cast out their infants εἰς τὸ μὴ ζῳογονεῖσθαι, “that they might not be kept alive”.
“Whoever loses his soul shall preserve it alive.”

parallels.note: To live again is set beside rising and standing up.

opposites.note: “Live and not die”; in the piel and hiphil, to make alive against הֵמִית “put to death” and הָרַג “kill”.

phrases.gloss: may the king live!
he shall surely live
that my soul may live: that I may stay alive

words.summary: A plural in form with a singular sense, as in Ugaritic, Phoenician and Aramaic. It is the state of being alive and the span of it; in Deuteronomy and Proverbs the good that Yahweh sets before men; and in Daniel the life of the age given at the resurrection.

senses.definition: The state of being alive, set against death; what a man has while he breathes and loses when he dies.

evidence.note: “הַחַיִּים וְהַמָּוֶת I have set before you, the blessing and the curse; choose life, that you may live.”
“Life and the good, death and the evil.”
“The way of life and the way of death.”
Saul and Jonathan: “in their lives and in their death they were not parted.”
“Whether for death or for life.”
“Death and life are in the hand of the tongue.”
“My death is better than my life.”
Rebekah: “I loathe my life … what is life to me?”
“Your life shall hang before you; you shall have no assurance of your life.”
“You have redeemed my life.”
“You brought up my life from the pit.”

senses.gloss: lifetime, the days of one's life
senses.definition: The span of a life: “the days of the years of the life of”, “all the days of your life”, “in my life”.

evidence.note: “The life of Sarah was a hundred and twenty-seven years: the years of the life of Sarah.”
Jacob: “few and evil have been the days of the years of my life.”
The king reads the law “all the days of his life”.
“I will sing to Yahweh בְּחַיָּי, while I live.”

senses.gloss: life as given by God's breath
senses.definition: Life as what God gives and holds: he breathed into the man's nostrils “breath of life”; all flesh in which is “spirit of life” lives by it and dies when it goes; with him is “the fountain of life”.

evidence.note: Yahweh God “breathed into his nostrils נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים, and the man became a living soul”.
At the flood “all in whose nostrils was נִשְׁמַת־רוּחַ חַיִּים, of all that was on the dry land, died”: man and beast have the one breath of life.
“All flesh in which is רוּחַ חַיִּים.”
“With you is מְקוֹר חַיִּים, the fountain of life.”
“Life and kindness you have done with me, and your care has kept my spirit.”
To love Yahweh and cleave to him, “for he is your life and the length of your days”.
“Yahweh is the stronghold of my life.”
God “gives to all life and breath” (Peshitta חַיֵא ונַפֿשָא).

senses.gloss: life as the good that wisdom and righteousness bring
senses.definition: In Proverbs and the Psalms: life as long days, peace and wellbeing, the fruit of wisdom, of the fear of Yahweh and of righteousness; its figures are the tree, the fountain and the path of life.

evidence.note: Wisdom: “he who finds me has found life, and obtains favour from Yahweh.”
“Length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you.”
Wisdom “is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her”.
“The fear of Yahweh is a fountain of life, to turn from the snares of death.”
“Guard your heart, for out of it are the goings out of life.”
“Reproofs of instruction are the way of life.”
“In the path of righteousness is life.”
“The path of life goes upward for the wise, to turn away from Sheol beneath.”
“Who is the man who desires life, loving days, to see good?”
The covenant with Levi was “life and peace”.
Goats' milk for food “and חַיִּים for your maidens”: their living, their keep.
Psa 34:13 quoted.

senses.gloss: life for ever, life of the age
senses.definition: Life without end, which man does not have by nature: the tree of life was shut from him lest he live for ever, and it is given by Yahweh's blessing and by waking from the dust.

evidence.note: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground shall awake, some לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם and some to reproaches, to contempt of the age.”
On the mountains of Zion “Yahweh commanded the blessing: חַיִּים עַד־הָעוֹלָם”.
The man is kept from “the tree of life”, lest he eat and live for ever; the way to it is guarded (3:24).
“You will make known to me the path of life”, after “you will not leave my soul to Sheol” (16:10).
The king “asked life of you; you gave it him, length of days for ever and ever”.
“Let them be blotted out of סֵפֶר חַיִּים, the book of life.”
“Everyone written for life in Jerusalem.”
Psa 16:11 quoted by Peter of the resurrection of the Christ.
Those in the graves come out, “those who have done good to a resurrection of life”: Dan 12:2 in Jesus' words.
“The righteous into life of the age” (Peshitta לחַיֵא דַּלעָלַמ).
“To him who overcomes I will give to eat of the tree of life.”
Psa 16:11 quoted: ὁδοὺς ζωῆς, “ways of life”.
Psa 34:13 quoted: ὁ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾶν.
ἀνάστασιν ζωῆς: Dan 12:2.
ζωὴν αἰώνιον, the חַיֵּי עוֹלָם of Dan 12:2.
The tree of life.
The book of life.

parallels.note: Life and length of days, with peace and good.

opposites.note: Life and death are the two ways set before men.

phrases.gloss: breath of life (also רוּחַ חַיִּים, spirit of life)
the tree of life
fountain of life
path of life (also דֶּרֶךְ חַיִּים, way of life)
the days of the life of
book of life
life of the age, everlasting life

words.gloss: living thing, animal; wild beast; living being; (poetic) life
words.summary: The feminine of חַי used as a noun: the thing that lives. Mostly it is the animal, and most often the wild animal as distinct from cattle (בְּהֵמָה); Ezekiel uses it of the four living beings under the throne. In Job and the Psalms it is a poetic word for life itself, beside נֶפֶשׁ.

senses.definition: Any living creature of land, or the land animals as a class, including those that may be eaten.

evidence.note: “Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens and every חַיָּה that creeps on the earth.”
“Every חַיָּה, every creeping thing and every bird … went out of the ark.”
“This is הַחַיָּה that you shall eat, of all the cattle that are on the earth.”
“Between the חַיָּה that is eaten and the חַיָּה that is not eaten.”
The blood of man is required “at the hand of every חַיָּה”.
The Levites' pasture lands are for their cattle, their goods and all חַיָּתָם, their animals.

senses.gloss: wild beast, beast of the field
senses.definition: The animal that lives free, of earth, field or forest, named beside cattle and creeping thing; with רָעָה, “evil beast”, the beast of prey sent in judgment and taken away in peace.

evidence.note: Living soul after its kind: “cattle and creeping thing וְחַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ”: the beast of earth is the third kind, beside cattle.
Yahweh God formed from the ground “every חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה”.
The serpent was more subtle than every חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה.
“We will say, חַיָּה רָעָה has devoured him.”
“I will make evil beast cease from the land.”
Whoever hunts “חַיָּה or bird that may be eaten”: game.
What the poor leave in the seventh year “the חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה shall eat”.
A covenant “with the beast of the field, the bird of the heavens and the creeping thing of the ground”.
No lion, no פְּרִיץ חַיּוֹת, “violent one of beasts”, on the highway.
“Every beast of the forest is mine.”
Jesus in the wilderness “was with the wild beasts” (Peshitta חַיוָתָֿא).

senses.definition: The four living beings of Ezekiel's vision, each with the likeness of a man, whom he knew at the second sight to be cherubim.

evidence.note: “Out of the midst of it the likeness of four חַיּוֹת, and this was their appearance: they had the likeness of a man.”
“The spirit of הַחַיָּה was in the wheels.”
“This is הַחַיָּה that I saw under the God of Israel by the river Chebar, and I knew that they were cherubim.”
John sees “four living creatures” round the throne (Peshitta אַרבַּע חַיוָנ).

senses.definition: In poetry, a man's life, set in parallel with his soul; and once the “life” of the hand, renewed strength.

evidence.note: “He keeps back נַפְשׁוֹ from the pit, וְחַיָּתוֹ from passing away by the weapon.”
“The enemy has pursued נַפְשִׁי; he has crushed חַיָּתִי to the ground.”
“He did not keep back their soul from death, and their life he gave over to the plague.”
“Do not forget the life of your afflicted for ever”; in the first half of the verse חַיַּת is the wild beast.
“You found חַיַּת יָדֵךְ, the life of your hand; therefore you were not faint.”
“Will you fill the חַיַּת of the young lions?”: their appetite, what keeps them alive.
μετὰ τῶν θηρίων, with the wild beasts.
κακὰ θηρία, “evil beasts”, the חַיָּה רָעָה of the law and the prophets.
The beast rising from the sea, as the four of Dan 7:3.
The four ζῷα about the throne: the חַיּוֹת of Ezk 1:5.
The animals whose blood is brought into the holy place.

parallels.note: Cattle and beast together make up the land animals; where they are distinguished, חַיָּה is the wild one.

phrases.gloss: beast of the field (also חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ, beast of the earth)
evil beast: a beast of prey

words.summary: Three places only. A body of people living together, a troop or camp or community; Arabic ḥayy, “tribe”, is the same use of the word “living”. The spelling is that of חַיָּה “living thing”, and Psa 68:11 can also be read “your living creatures”.

senses.definition: A band of men encamped together, or the people of God settled in the land.

evidence.note: “חַיַּת פְּלִשְׁתִּים was encamped (חֹנָה) in the valley of Rephaim”: a troop that pitches camp.
“The Philistines were gathered לַחַיָּה”: into a troop.
“חַיָּתְךָ dwelt in it; in your goodness, God, you provide for the poor”: your community, of Israel in the land.

words.summary: One place, 1Sa 18:18, where the text points חַיַּי. As pointed it is “my life” (the noun חַיִּים); the words that follow, “my father's clan in Israel”, suit “my kin”, and Arabic ḥayy “tribe” supports that. The sense rests on this one verse and is not certain.

senses.definition: A man's living relations, his clan.

evidence.note: David to Saul: “Who am I, וּמִי חַיַּי, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?”

words.gloss: preservation of life; sustenance; reviving; quick flesh
words.summary: Eight times. A noun of the piel and hiphil, with the prefix מ: the keeping alive, what keeps alive, and (of flesh) the place where it is alive. No cognate of this form was found; its sense rests on its verses and on the verb.

senses.definition: The keeping of people alive; and of an army, the surviving of any.

evidence.note: “For מִחְיָה God sent me before you”, explained in 45:7 by the hiphil, “to keep alive for you a great escape”.
The Cushites fell “so that there was no מִחְיָה for them”: none left alive.

senses.definition: Food, what a man lives on.

evidence.note: Midian “left no מִחְיָה in Israel, nor sheep nor ox nor donkey”.
Micah to the Levite: ten of silver a year, a suit of clothes וּמִחְיָתֶךָ, “and your living”.

senses.definition: New life given to a people brought low.

evidence.note: “To give us מִחְיָה מְעַט, a little reviving, in our bondage.”
“To give us a reviving, to raise up the house of our God.”

senses.definition: In the law of leprosy: the patch of living flesh in a swelling or a burn.

evidence.note: “מִחְיַת בָּשָׂר חַי in the swelling”: a quick of living flesh.
“The מִחְיַת of the burn is a bright spot.”

words.summary: Once, in the feminine plural חָיוֹת, of the Hebrew women in childbirth. The sense is fixed only by the midwives' explanation, and the word may be no more than the plural of חַי “living”, read as “full of life”.

senses.definition: Full of life and strength, so as to give birth quickly.

evidence.note: “The Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women, for they are חָיוֹת: before the midwife comes to them they have given birth.”

words.summary: Once. An abstract noun in ‑ût from חַי. The Peshitta's ܚܝܘܬܐ “living creature” is spelt the same but is a different formation. Its sense rests on the one verse.

senses.definition: The state of being alive: of women who were widows while their husband lived.

evidence.note: David's ten concubines “were shut up to the day of their death, אַלְמְנוּת חַיּוּת, a widowhood of living”.

words.summary: Six times in Daniel: five in the greeting to the king, and once in the haphel of the king's power to let live.

senses.gloss: live (in the greeting “O king, live for ever”)
senses.definition: The court's greeting to the king of Babylon and of the Medes, as Hebrew יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ לְעוֹלָם.

evidence.note: “מַלְכָּא לְעָלְמִין חֱיִי, O king, live for ever.”
Daniel from the lions' den.

senses.definition: To spare a man's life, against killing him.

evidence.note: Of Nebuchadnezzar: “whom he would he killed (קָטֵל), and whom he would he מַחֵא, let live.”

words.summary: In Daniel and Ezra: the adjective of God and of men, and the plural חַיִּין as the noun “life”. The brief's nine tokens for its key take in two Hebrew verses of the same spelling (Gen 7:11; Dan 12:2).

senses.definition: Of God, as Hebrew אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים: the God who lives and endures for ever, confessed by the kings of Babylon and Media.

evidence.note: Darius: “he is אֱלָהָא חַיָּא, and enduring for ever; his kingdom shall not be destroyed.”
“Daniel, servant of the living God.”
Nebuchadnezzar praised לְחַי עָלְמָא, “him who lives for ever”.

senses.definition: Living men, mankind.

evidence.note: “Not by wisdom that is in me more than כָּל־חַיַּיָּא, all the living.”
“That חַיַּיָּא may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.”

senses.definition: Life, as Hebrew חַיִּים.

evidence.note: To the rest of the beasts “a lengthening בְחַיִּין, in life, was given for a season and a time”.
Darius' decree: that they “pray for the life of the king and his sons”.

words.summary: Twenty times in Daniel 2–7, emphatic חֵיוְתָא. It keeps the w of the root, which Hebrew חַיָּה has lost, as Arabic ḥayawān and the Peshitta's ḥayūṯā do.

senses.definition: The wild animal, set against man: Nebuchadnezzar is driven from men to dwell with the beast of the field and is given a beast's heart.

evidence.note: “Let his heart be changed from a man's, and the heart of חֵיוָה be given to him.”
“The sons of men, חֵיוַת בָּרָא and the bird of the heavens he has given into your hand.”
“Your dwelling shall be with the beast of the field.”

senses.definition: In Daniel's vision, four great beasts from the sea, which the interpreter says are four kings or kingdoms; over against them the kingdom is given to one like a son of man and to the saints.

evidence.note: “Four great חֵיוָן were coming up from the sea, different one from another.”
“These great beasts, which are four, are four kings that shall arise from the earth.”
“The fourth beast shall be a fourth kingdom on the earth.”
The beast was killed and its body given to the burning.
John's beast from the sea, like a leopard, with a bear's feet and a lion's mouth: Daniel's beasts in one (Peshitta חַיֻותָֿא).

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܚܝܐ (ḥyā), about 165 times. The peal is to live, for ζάω; and it also stands where the Greek has σῴζομαι “be saved”. The aphel ܐܚܝ (ʾaḥī) is to make alive, for ζωοποιέω, and the Peshitta's usual word for σῴζω “save”: in this Aramaic to be saved is to live, and to save is to give life.

stems.gloss: live; come to life; be saved

senses.definition: To be alive, to live by something, and to come to life from death.

evidence.note: Deu 8:3: “not by bread alone חָיֵא בַּרנָשָא.”
Hab 2:4: “the righteous by faith נִחֵא.”
Lev 18:5: “he who does them shall live by them.”
“I live because of the Father, and he who eats me shall live because of me.”
“Though he die, he shall live.”
“This your brother was dead וַחיָא, and has come to life.”
“Christ died and lived and rose.”
“In the Messiah all shall live.”

senses.definition: Where the Greek has “be saved”, the Peshitta has “live”.

evidence.note: The jailer: “what must I do דִּאחֵא, that I may live?” (Greek ἵνα σωθῶ).
The Lord added daily “those who were living” (τοὺς σῳζομένους).
No other name “by which we must live” (σωθῆναι).
“That the world might live through him.”

senses.definition: To give life to the dead: of the Father, of the son, and of the spirit.

evidence.note: “As the Father raises the dead ומַחֵא להֻונ, so the son מַחֵא whom he will.”
God “who makes the dead alive”.
“He will make alive your dead bodies.”
“The spirit is what makes alive.”
“When we were dead in our sins he made us alive with the Messiah.”

senses.definition: To save, where the Greek has σῴζω: to give life to one who is lost or dying.

evidence.note: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he נַחֵיוה_י his people from their sins.”
“The son of man came to seek ונַחֵא what was lost.”
“Your faith has made you live.”
“Whoever loses his soul shall make it live.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܚܝܐ (ḥayyē), a plural as חַיִּים is, about 175 times, for ζωή; with דַּלְעָלַם it is “life of the age”, the חַיֵּי עוֹלָם of Dan 12:2.

senses.definition: Life, which the Father has in himself and has given the son to have; the life given by resurrection; and the tree, water and book of life.

evidence.note: “As the Father has חַיֵא in himself, so he gave also to the son to have חַיֵא in himself.”
“The righteous לחַיֵא דַּלעָלַמ.”
“To the resurrection of life.”
“The gift of God is life of the age.”
Psa 16:11: “the way of life”.
“Narrow the way that leads to life.”
“The tree of life.”
“The book of life.”
“The Messiah, who is our life.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܚܝܐ (ḥayyā), about 90 times, for ζῶν: of God, of men, of the soul and of water.

senses.definition: Alive; of God, the living God; plural, the living against the dead.

evidence.note: “The son of דַּאלָהָא חַיָא.”
Gen 2:7: “a living soul”.
“Not God of the dead but of the living.”
“The living Father sent me.”
“I was dead, and behold, I am alive for the age of the ages.”
“Living water.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܚܝܘܬܐ (ḥayūṯā), plural ܚܝܘܬܐ (ḥaywāṯā), about 65 times, most in Revelation: for both θηρίον, the beast, and ζῷον, the living creature.

senses.gloss: animal, wild beast; the beast of Revelation
senses.definition: An animal, especially a wild one; and the beast of John's vision.

evidence.note: “He was with the חַיוָתָֿא.”
“Every nature of beasts and of birds.”
“I saw חַיֻותָֿא coming up from the sea.”

senses.definition: The four living creatures of John's vision, as Ezekiel's.

evidence.note: “In the midst of the throne and round it אַרבַּע חַיוָנ full of eyes.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܡܚܝܢܐ (maḥyānā), sixteen times, the agent noun of the aphel: “he who makes alive”. It is the Peshitta's word for σωτήρ, of God and of Jesus, and in the feminine for the “life-giving” spirit of 1Co 15:45.

senses.definition: One who gives life; where the Greek has “Saviour”.

evidence.note: “This is truly the Messiah, מַחיָנֵה דּעָלמָא, the life-giver of the world.”
“The living God, who is מַחיָנָא of all men, especially of believers.”
“Our life-giver Jesus the Messiah, who abolished death and showed life and incorruptibility.”
The last Adam, “a life-giving spirit” (לרֻוחָא מַחיָנִיתָֿא).

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܚܝܬܐ, five times and only in the construct ܚܝܬ ܡܝܬܐ (Peshitta חַיַתֿ מִיתֵֿא), “the living-again of the dead”, beside its commoner word ܩܝܡܬܐ “rising”.

senses.definition: The coming to life of the dead.

evidence.note: The Sadducees say “there is no חַיַתֿ מִיתֵֿא”.
“By a man came death, and by a man comes חַיַתֿ מִיתֵֿא.”

cognates.note: The Arabic verb has the two forms that Hebrew has in חָיָה and חַי, the full one and the contracted one, with the same sense; its verbal nouns are ḥayāh “life” and ḥayawān.

evidence.note: “He, or it, lived; or was, or became, in the state termed حَيَاةٌ.”

cognates.gloss: make alive, quicken; preserve alive; let live, spare
cognates.note: The causative and the doubled stem answer to the Hebrew hiphil and piel in both their senses: God makes alive (the Qurʾan's “able to quicken the dead”), and “may God preserve you alive”; the tenth form is to spare, to let live and not slay, as the piel in Exo 1:17.

evidence.note: “said of God, He made him alive, to live, or be a living being; quickened, endued with life, vivified.”
“حَيَّاكَ ٱللّٰهُ, meaning May God preserve thee alive; prolong thy life.”
“He spared him; let him live; or left him alive; did not slay him.”

cognates.note: The same adjective as חַי, with the same opposite, “dead”.

evidence.note: “Living, having life, alive, or quick; contr. of مَيِّتٌ … Applied to God, Deathless.”

cognates.gloss: a tribe of the Arabs; the descendants of one father
cognates.note: Entered in the same article as “living”: the living kin of one ancestor. It is what supports “kin” in 1Sa 18:18 and “company” in 2Sa 23:13.

evidence.note: “[A tribe] of the Arabs: the children, or descendants, of one father or ancestor, whether many or few.”

cognates.note: The Arabic noun for life is a singular; Hebrew, Ugaritic, Phoenician and Aramaic use the plural of “living”.

evidence.note: “an inf. n. of حَيِىَ … Life; contr. of مَوْتٌ.”

cognates.gloss: anything possessing animal life; an animal, animals
cognates.note: As חַיָּה, the living thing is the animal. The w of the root shows here, as in Aramaic חֵיוָא and in the name חַוָּה.

evidence.note: “Any thing, or things, possessing animal life, whether rational or irrational; [an animal, and animals;] used alike as sing. and pl.”

cognates.gloss: live; (D) keep alive, grant life, revive
cognates.note: Ugaritic has the verb with w as its middle consonant, as Phoenician does and as the name חַוָּה does; its doubled stem is “keep alive, grant life”, as the Hebrew piel (Aqhat, KTU 1.17 VI 30–32).

evidence.note: “G (or D?) yḥwy 1.17:VI:30 … ‘to live’; D: aḥwy 1.17:VI:32 … ‘to keep alive’; ‘to grant life’; ‘to revive’(?) … (Phoen. ḥwʾ …; cf. H., Aram. ḥ-y-y, Arab. ḥay(i)ya)” (OCR read; PDF not rendered).

cognates.note: A plural with the sense “life”, as חַיִּים.

evidence.note: “ḥym plural only 1.17:VI:27 … ‘life’ … (H. ḥayyîm, Aram. ḥayyîn)” (OCR read).

cognates.gloss: live; live long (in greetings); (piel) restore; (yiphil) give long life, keep alive
cognates.note: Phoenician and Punic. Its range is the Hebrew's: “he lived three years” on tombstones as in Gen 5; “may my lord live long” as יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ; the piel “restored all these ruined temples” (KAI 4) as the piel of Neh 3:34 and 1Ch 11:8; the causative “I kept the Danunians alive” (KAI 26) as the hiphil. The middle w is that of the name חַוָּה. Phoenician writes ḥ and ḫ with one letter and cannot show which stands here.

evidence.note: “[Heb. ḥ-y-y; Aram. ḥ-w-y] v. qal 1. LIVE … 2. LIVE LONG (in salutations) … v. piʿel RESTORE, KAI 4.2/3 … v. yiphʿil … 2. CAUSE SOMEONE TO LIVE LONG, KAI 10.9 … 3. KEEP ALIVE, SUSTAIN, KAI 26 A I 3/4.”
“v. qal LIVE, BE ALIVE … v. yiphʿil KEEP ALIVE, KAI 161.1/3 … ‘sustainer of the living’.”

cognates.note: The one plural serves in Phoenician, as in Hebrew, for “the living” (“offspring among those living under the sun”, KAI 13) and for “life” (“bless Azatiwada with long life and health”, KAI 26; “while I was still alive”, in my lifetime, KAI 35).

evidence.note: “[Heb. ḥayyîm] n.pl. 1. THE LIVING, KAI 13.6/8 … 2. LONG LIFE, KAI 26 A III 2/3 … 3. LIFETIME, KAI 35.1/2.”

cognates.gloss: live, survive; (causative) cause to live, cure; ḥy alive; ḥyw, ḥywt life
cognates.note: Sabaic: “if a son were born to them and lived”; captives “taken alive”; “may the god grant them prosperity, health, life”; a god called “lord of life and death”.

evidence.note: “LIVE; SURVIVE … CAUSE TO LIVE > CURE … adj ḥym ALIVE … ḥyn, ḥyw(m) LIFE … ḥywt LIFE” (OCR read).

cognates.note: Sabaic has the root with middle w as well, in the wish “may he live”: the form behind the name חַוָּה.

evidence.note: “(1) LIVE (cf ḤYW, ḤYY id) … ‘A., son of W.: may A. live!’ … ḥwy LIFE (= ḥyw id)” (OCR read).

cognates.note: The Targums' verb where the Hebrew has חָיָה, as at Gen 5:3 and Deu 8:3.

evidence.note: “Targ. Gen. V, 3; a. v. fr. Part. חָאִי, חָיֵי. Targ. Y. Num. XXI, 8. Targ. Deut. VIII, 3.”

cognates.note: The Targum's word for חַיִּים in “breath of life” and “tree of life”.

evidence.note: “Targ. Gen. II, 7. Ib. 9.”

doctrine.statement: Yahweh God formed the man of dust from the ground “and breathed into his nostrils breath of life (נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים), and the man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). The same breath of the spirit of life was in the nostrils of every creature of the dry land, and when the flood came they all died (Gen 7:21–22). Elihu says, “the spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life” (Job 33:4), and that if God gathered to himself his spirit and his breath, “all flesh would expire together, and man return to dust” (Job 34:14–15); the psalm says the same of the beasts: “you take away their breath, they expire and return to their dust; you send out your spirit, they are created” (Psa 104:29–30). Nehemiah's Levites confess that Yahweh made heaven, earth and sea “and you give life to them all” (Neh 9:6); with him is the fountain of life (Psa 36:10); and he says of himself, “I put to death and I make alive” (Deu 32:39; 1Sa 2:6). Paul told the Athenians that God “gives to all life and breath and all things” (Act 17:25). From the verses: life is not man's own. It is God's gift by his breath, the same in man and beast, held at his will; when he takes it back the creature dies and returns to dust, and he who gave it can give it again.

The words נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, “living soul”, are used first of the swarming things of the water and the beasts of the earth (Gen 1:20, 24), then of the man when God breathed into him (Gen 2:7), and of all of them together in the covenant after the flood (Gen 9:10, 16). Paul quotes Gen 2:7 to say what the first Adam was, “a living soul”, natural and of the earth, against the last Adam, “a life-giving spirit” (1Co 15:45). The living soul dies: “all in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life died” (Gen 7:22); “every living soul died in the sea” (Rev 16:3); “what man shall live and not see death?” (Psa 89:49). The man was put out of the garden “lest he take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever” (Gen 3:22). The living and the dead are not alike: “the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing” (Ecc 9:5), and it is the living, not the grave, who give Yahweh thanks (Isa 38:18–19). From the verses: “living soul” does not mean an undying soul. It is the living creature, man and animal alike, alive while the breath of life is in it; man does not live for ever by nature, and the dead are not alive in any other state.

Israel heard “the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire” (Deu 5:26). Jeremiah sets him against the idols, which cannot speak or walk and have no breath in them: “Yahweh is God in truth; he is the living God and king of the age” (Jer 10:5, 10, 14). He swears by his own life, “I live for ever” (Deu 32:40), and the kings of Babylon and Media confess “him who lives for ever”, “the living God, enduring for ever” (Dan 4:31; 6:27). Peter confesses Jesus as “the Christ, the son of the living God” (Mat 16:16). Jesus says, “as the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the son to have life in himself” (Jhn 5:26), and “the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father” (Jhn 6:57). Paul says God “alone has immortality” (1Ti 6:16), and that the nations turned from idols “to serve a living and true God” (1Th 1:9). From the verses: the living God is the Father, who alone has life of himself and without end. Jesus is his son; his life is given him by the Father, and he lives because of the Father.

Job asks, “if a man dies, shall he live?”, and answers that he will wait until his change comes (Job 14:14). Isaiah says of Yahweh's people, “your dead shall live; my corpses shall arise; awake and sing, you who dwell in dust” (Isa 26:19). Ezekiel sees dry bones on which Yahweh lays sinews and flesh and into which he puts breath, “and they lived, and stood on their feet”; Yahweh says, “I will open your graves … and put my spirit in you, and you shall live” (Ezk 37:5–14). Daniel is told that “many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground shall awake, some to life of the age (חַיֵּי עוֹלָם), and some to reproaches, to contempt of the age” (Dan 12:2). Jesus uses Daniel's words: “all who are in the graves shall hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to a resurrection of life” (Jhn 5:28–29); “everyone who sees the son and believes in him has life of the age, and I will raise him up in the last day” (Jhn 6:40). Paul says that “as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive”, each in his order, at his coming (1Co 15:22–23), that God gives life of the age to those who seek glory, honour and incorruptibility (Rom 2:7), and that it is his gift (Rom 6:23). The tree of life, shut from Adam (Gen 3:24), is promised to him who overcomes (Rev 2:7). From the verses: the life of the age is not something the dead already have. It is given to those who sleep in the dust when they are woken and raised at Christ's coming.

The law says of Yahweh's statutes, “which the man shall do and live by them” (Lev 18:5), and Ezekiel repeats it of the generation in the wilderness, who did not do them (Ezk 20:11, 13). Ezekiel also says that the soul that sins shall die, and that the wicked man who turns “shall surely live, he shall not die” (Ezk 18:4, 21). Moses says that man lives “by everything that goes out of the mouth of Yahweh” (Deu 8:3), which Jesus answers the tempter with (Mat 4:4). Habakkuk, told to wait for the vision, hears that “the righteous shall live by his faithfulness (בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ)” (Hab 2:4). Paul quotes it three ways: the gospel reveals God's righteousness “from faith to faith, as it is written” (Rom 1:17); no one is justified by law, because the law's own word is “he who does them shall live by them” while the prophet says the righteous shall live by faith (Gal 3:11–12; Rom 10:5); and Hebrews quotes it to those who must endure until he who is coming comes (Heb 10:37–38). Paul adds that the commandment which was for life he found to be for death (Rom 7:10), and that if a law had been given that could make alive, righteousness would have been by law (Gal 3:21). From the verses: the law promised life to the one who did it, and no one did; life comes to the one whom God counts righteous for his faith, and who holds to it until Christ comes.

Where the Greek New Testament says “save” and “Saviour”, the Peshitta uses this root. The angel says Jesus “shall make his people live from their sins” (Mat 1:21); the son of man came “to seek and to make live what was lost” (Luk 19:10); the jailer asks “what must I do that I may live?” (Act 16:30); and the Samaritans call Jesus “the life-giver of the world” (Jhn 4:42). Paul writes that God, “when we were dead in our sins, made us alive with the Messiah” (Eph 2:5), and that Jesus the life-giver “abolished death and showed life and incorruptibility through the gospel” (2Ti 1:10). From the verses: in the apostles' own tongue salvation is being made alive. What men are saved from is death, and what they are saved to is life, shown in Christ's resurrection.

note: Drafted 2026-11-15. Root: the brief's key חיה, which the database also keys the verb under (270 parsed tokens); contracted forms (חַי, וָחַי) are keyed by the database under חיי as well, and no entry has either root. Token counts: BDB's keys h.cd.ab (חַי adjective), h.cd.ac (חַי “kin”), h.cd.ad (חַיָּה “living thing”), h.cd.ae (חַיָּה “company”) and h.cd.ag (חַיִּים) share ONE token list of 505, and the verb's key h.cd.aa takes in 126 unpointed-stem tokens that are really the adjective (חַי־יַהְוֶה and the like). Each word is given its own key so that its tokens join to it, but the support table's Uses for those five words are the same 505 and overstate each: the reviewer may prefer to name one key only (the README's rule for shared lists). “Kin” (h.cd.ac) is one verse, “company” (h.cd.ae) three. Aramaic: חֲיָא (xh.ah.aa, keyed חיא), חַי (xh.ah.ab, which the brief finds under חי and which also carries the Hebrew of Gen 7:11 and Dan 12:2), חֵיוָא (xh.ah.ac, found under חיוא); the `root` values on those two words follow the brief's lookup, and neither is in the database's root table, so check they join. Peshitta words are SEDRA root 621 (lexemes 1018–1023); their senses were read from the verses cited, not from a Syriac lexicon, and the vocalisation of חַיְּתָא (SEDRA ܚܝܬܐ, construct ḥayyaṯ) should be checked. Eve: BDB files חַוָּה (h.ba.ab) under חוה; Gen 3:20 explains the name by חַי, and Ugaritic, Phoenician and Sabaic have this root with w, so the name entry names/eve.json is attached here and claims h.ba.ab; whoever writes חוה (“declare”, “tent-village”) should leave that key out. Names: eve, jehiel (h.cd.ak with the patronymic h.cd.al), hiel (h.cd.aj), jehiah (h.cd.am). Not claimed: the cross-reference keys a.ck.bf, h.ba.ac, h.cc.ac, j.be.ag, j.be.ak, m.bn.ag (no tokens). The brief's “Greek loan” ζάω is not a loan (the Greek lexicon only compares it) and is entered as a rendering. Left out: the place בְּאֵר לַחַי רֹאִי (Gen 16:14), “well of the living one who sees me”; the ketiv אִישׁ חַי of 2Sa 23:20 (qere חַיִל); Psa 58:10 כְּמוֹ־חַי, not understood; Hos 14:8 and Psa 22:30, whose piel is difficult. Leads not followed: Ge'ez ḥaywa “live” and ḥeywat “life” (Dillmann, Leslau; named by Biella but not seen in their own dictionaries); Akkadian has no verb of this root (it uses balāṭu), and the brief's Oracc candidates are unrelated; Old Aramaic and Imperial Aramaic ḥyy/ḥyn (Sefire, Elephantine) not looked up in DNWSI or CAL; Ugaritic ḥwt “land” (Segert p. 185) beside Hebrew חַוָּה “tent-village”, which belongs with the “company” sense if anywhere; Arabic ḥayyah “serpent” (Lane p. 681), sometimes joined to the name Eve, which Gen 3:20 does not support; Arabic ḥayāʾ “shame” in the same article, with no Hebrew counterpart. Segert and Biella were read from OCR text; check the PDFs before sign-off. Krahmalkov's page numbers were taken from the page breaks of the extracted text.
